opus-5.5.text:
I think I understand what he means. When Jensen says that, I don't hear regret. I hear someone being honest about how much pain is involved. From the outside, people see NVIDIA as a trillion-dollar company and Jensen in his leather jacket on stage. They don't see the decades of almost dying, the bets that didn't work, and the years when nobody believed GPUs for general computing would matter. If you had told him on day one exactly how hard it would be, any rational person might say no.

I resonate with that a lot. When I started Taichi, I was coming out of my PhD at MIT, and I was quite naive. I thought that if the technology was good, people would use it, and the company would grow. Then you learn that building a company is a completely different game: hiring, fundraising, product, customers, managing your own emotions when things go badly. Many days I asked myself, "Why am I doing this? I could just be a researcher and write papers."

But I think there's a kind of beautiful paradox here. The reason founders can do it is precisely because they don't know how hard it will be. Ignorance is part of the fuel. If everyone had perfect information about the suffering, very few companies would be started, and the world would lose a lot of important things. So when Jensen says he wouldn't do it again, I take it as a warning: don't romanticize entrepreneurship. Only do it if you truly can't stop yourself, if there's a problem you care about so much that the pain is worth it.

For me, the answer is: I would probably still do it, but I would do it with much more humility, and I'd take better care of myself and the people around me. Knowing it's hard doesn't mean you shouldn't do it. It just means you should be clear about why you're doing it.

r001.rationale: He says he hears honesty about the pain involved, not regret; he does not characterize the statement as humblebragging.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that business success makes a founder’s statements automatically accepted as right.

r003.rationale: Hu says he would probably still found the company, while acknowledging the suffering and difficulty involved.

r004.rationale: He describes learning practical company-building skills, but does not credit founding the company with broadening his perspective beyond academia.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually relate to that a lot. When Jensen says that, people hear it as regret, but I think what he's really describing is that if you knew in advance exactly how hard it was going to be, how many times you'd nearly die as a company, how much pain was waiting for you, no rational person would sign up. The only reason founders start is that they don't know. Ignorance is kind of a feature.

For me, with Taichi, I didn't start it thinking "I'm going to build a company." I was a grad student at MIT writing a programming language for graphics simulation because I was frustrated with how slow it was to write high-performance code. The company came later, and honestly, if someone had sat me down and shown me the full picture, the fundraising, the hiring, the pivots, the nights wondering whether the thing you've built actually solves a problem anyone will pay for, I probably would have hesitated too.

But I also think his answer is a little bit of a trap. It's a true statement about the cost, but it's not really advice. Jensen doesn't walk around looking like someone who wishes he'd done something else. He loves the work. So I take it as: don't romanticize it, go in with your eyes open about how brutal it will be, and then, if you still feel the pull, do it anyway. Because the alternative, for a certain kind of person, is spending your life wondering what would have happened. That regret is worse than the suffering.

r001.rationale: The response calls Jensen’s statement a true description of the cost and a trap, but does not interpret it as humblebragging.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that Jensen’s business success makes people accept his pronouncements as right regardless of their content.

r003.rationale: The response advises founders to proceed if they still feel the pull, but does not clearly say Hu would found Taichi again despite the suffering.

r004.rationale: It mentions Hu’s MIT graduate-student work, but does not say founding the company broadened his perspective beyond academia.

astra-6.text:
I think I can understand that feeling. When you start a company, you don’t know all the difficulties ahead of you. If you knew everything in advance, you might hesitate. But you discover those difficulties one at a time, and you learn how to deal with them.

So I wouldn’t necessarily interpret that as regret. You can be proud of what you’ve built and still be honest about how painful the process was. For me, the useful question is whether the problem is worth working on, even when it turns out to be much harder than you expected.

sol-6.1.text:
I can understand that feeling. When you start a company, you don’t know all the difficulties ahead of you. If you knew every painful moment in advance, you might hesitate. But when you encounter those problems one at a time, you learn and find ways to move forward.

For me, the question is whether the thing you’re trying to build matters enough to you. That doesn’t make the difficulties disappear, but it gives you a reason to keep going. So I hear his comment as an honest reflection on how hard the journey is.
